title: FEV1 and vital capacity
summary: One hard breath out tells you both how much air the lungs hold and how fast it can leave.
objectives: Describe the forced vital capacity manoeuvre
Read vital capacity and FEV1 off a spirogram
Calculate FEV1/VC% and state its normal value
takeaways: VC = the most air you can breathe out after the deepest breath in.
FEV1 = the volume forced out in the first second of that breath.
FEV1/VC% is normally about 75% or more.

steps.title: A forced breath out
steps.text:
Spirometry is the commonest lung test. A nose clip closes the nose and the subject breathes through a mouthpiece into a spirometer; many modern ones use an airflow transducer (pneumotachograph) that measures flow and integrates it to volume.

For the forced vital capacity manoeuvre, take a few normal tidal breaths, inhale as deeply as possible, then blow out as hard, fast and completely as you can. It is used to diagnose asthma, COPD and cystic fibrosis.

check.q: What does an airflow transducer measure, and how does it get volume?
check.a: It measures flow; integrating flow over time gives volume.

steps.title: Reading VC and FEV1
steps.text:
On the spirogram the tidal breaths are small waves; the forced breath is one big swing. Vital capacity (VC) is its full height, read peak-to-peak from the top of the maximal inhalation to the bottom of the exhalation.

FEV1, the forced expiratory volume in one second, is how much of that air leaves in the first second after expiration starts. Healthy lungs empty most of their vital capacity in that first second.

check.a: The volume of air forcibly exhaled in the first second of a forced expiration that starts from full inspiration.

steps.title: The FEV1/VC ratio
steps.text:
Dividing one by the other gives FEV1/VC% (the Tiffeneau index): FEV1 ÷ VC × 100. Healthy adults blow out about 75% or more of their vital capacity in the first second.

Worked example: FEV1 3.6 L and VC 4.5 L gives 80%, a normal result. Because it is a ratio, it separates slow emptying (a low percentage) from small lungs (a normal percentage of a small VC).

check.q: FEV1 is 2.4 L and VC is 4.0 L. What is FEV1/VC%, and is it normal?
check.a: 60%, which is low (normal is about 75% or more).

practice.q: Vital capacity is read from the forced breath as:
choices: The volume in the first second
The height of one tidal wave
practice.why: From the top of the maximal inhalation to the bottom of the exhalation.

practice.q: A normal FEV1/VC% in a healthy adult is about:
practice.why: Most of the vital capacity leaves in the first second.

practice.q: Put the forced vital capacity manoeuvre in order
Name three diseases spirometry helps diagnose.
What is a pneumotachograph?
practice.a: An airflow transducer: it measures airflow, which is integrated to give volume.

practice.q: FEV1 3.6 L, VC 4.5 L: calculate FEV1/VC%.
What does a spirogram plot, and what does tidal volume look like on it?
practice.a: Volume against time; tidal volume shows as the small regular waves of quiet breathing.

title: Obstructive and restrictive disease
summary: Narrow airways empty slowly; stiff or small lungs hold less. Spirometry tells them apart.
objectives: Define pulmonary obstruction and restriction and list causes of each
Predict VC and FEV1/VC% in each pattern
Explain why phrenic nerve damage is restrictive
takeaways: Obstructive: VC normal or high, FEV1/VC% low, exhalation prolonged.
COPD by FEV1/VC%: ≥75 normal, 60–74 mild, 50–59 moderate, <50 severe.
Most COPD in North America is caused by smoking.

steps.title: Obstruction: air can't get out fast
steps.text:
Pulmonary obstruction means narrowed airways and higher airway resistance. Causes: asthma (bronchioles constrict and fill with mucus), bronchitis (inflamed bronchi with mucus hypersecretion) and emphysema (lost alveolar walls let small airways collapse).

In obstructive lung disease the VC is normal or even above normal, but the air leaves slowly: exhalation is prolonged and the FEV1/VC% is low.

check.q: In obstructive disease, what happens to VC and to FEV1/VC%?
check.a: VC is normal or above normal; FEV1/VC% is low.

steps.title: Restriction: the lungs can't fill
steps.text:
Pulmonary restriction means the lungs cannot fully inflate. Causes include pulmonary fibrosis (from cystic fibrosis, asbestosis or silicosis), scarring after chronic infection, pleural adhesions binding lung to chest wall, lung resection (removing part of a lung) and a paralysed diaphragm.

In restrictive lung disease the VC is reduced, but what air there is leaves quickly, so the FEV1/VC% is normal.

check.q: Why is FEV1/VC% normal in restrictive disease?
check.a: VC and FEV1 fall together: the airways are open, so the smaller volume still empties fast.

steps.title: COPD and its grades
steps.text:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is long-term obstruction, usually a mix of chronic bronchitis and emphysema. In North America most COPD is caused by smoking.

One simple grading uses FEV1/VC%: 75–100% normal, 60–74% mild, 50–59% moderate and below 50% severe.

check.q: An FEV1/VC% of 55% suggests what grade of COPD?

steps.title: The diaphragm and the phrenic nerve
steps.text:
The diaphragm is the main muscle of inspiration. Its motor supply is the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), which runs down through the neck and mediastinum to reach it.

Phrenic nerve damage paralyses the diaphragm on that side: it no longer descends, the lung cannot fully expand, and the pattern is restrictive.

check.q: Which nerve supplies the diaphragm, and from which spinal levels?

practice.q: Which is a restrictive cause?
practice.why: Asbestosis and silicosis cause fibrosis, which stiffens the lung.

practice.q: VC 5.0 L, FEV1/VC 55%. Pattern?
practice.why: Normal VC with a low ratio is obstruction.

practice.q: VC 2.8 L (well below predicted), FEV1/VC 85%. Pattern?
Put COPD grades from best to worst FEV1/VC%
List three obstructive diseases and what narrows the airway in each.
practice.a: Asthma: bronchoconstriction and mucus. Bronchitis: inflamed bronchi with excess mucus. Emphysema: lost alveolar walls let small airways collapse.

practice.q: What causes most COPD in North America?
Name four restrictive causes besides fibrosis.
practice.a: Scarring after chronic infection, pleural adhesions to the chest wall, lung resection, phrenic nerve damage paralysing the diaphragm.

practice.q: Where is the lesion in restriction: airways or lung tissue?
practice.a: Usually the lung tissue (parenchyma), pleura or chest wall, not the airways; obstruction affects the airways (bronchi, bronchioles) and, in emphysema, the alveoli.

title: Heart rate, fitness and the step test
summary: A fit heart beats slower at rest and settles faster after work; a step test turns that into a score.
objectives: Explain why trained people have a lower resting heart rate and faster recovery
Recognise the warning signs to stop exercising
Describe the Harvard step test and calculate a personal fitness index
takeaways: Aerobic training lowers resting heart rate and speeds heart-rate recovery.
Chest pain, pain down the left arm or faintness: stop.
PFI = seconds of exercise × 100 ÷ (2 × sum of three 30-s recovery pulse counts).
PFI: <55 poor, 55–64 low average, 65–79 high average, 80–89 good, ≥90 excellent.

steps.title: Resting heart rate and recovery
steps.text:
Aerobic exercise training enlarges the heart's stroke volume, so each beat moves more blood. The result is a lower resting heart rate in trained people than in sedentary ones.

A fit heart also returns to its resting rate faster after exercise. That heart rate recovery is a simple fitness index. The pulse is counted at the radial artery at the wrist or the common carotid artery in the neck.

check.q: Why is a trained athlete's resting heart rate lower?
check.a: Training raises stroke volume, so fewer beats per minute supply the same cardiac output.

steps.title: When to stop
steps.text:
Exercise raises the heart's own oxygen demand. If narrowed coronary arteries cannot meet it, the result is angina: chest pain from myocardial ischaemia, often radiating down the left arm.

Chest pain, pain spreading to the arm, or feeling faint are all reasons to stop at once.

check.q: What does chest pain radiating down the left arm during exercise suggest?

steps.title: The Harvard step test
steps.text:
The Harvard step test was devised at Harvard during the Second World War. The subject steps up and down a bench — 20 inches high for people 5 ft 8 in or taller, 16 inches for shorter people — at 30 complete step cycles per minute for 3 to 5 minutes.

Then they sit, and the pulse is counted for 30 seconds at 1–1.5, 2–2.5 and 3–3.5 minutes of recovery.

check.q: When are the three recovery pulse counts taken?
check.a: For 30 s each at 1–1.5, 2–2.5 and 3–3.5 minutes after stopping.

steps.title: Personal fitness index
steps.text:
Personal fitness index (PFI) = seconds of exercise × 100 ÷ (2 × the sum of the three pulse counts).

Example: 300 s of stepping, counts 60, 50 and 45 (sum 155): 30 000 ÷ 310 ≈ 97. Ratings: below 55 poor, 55–64 low average, 65–79 high average, 80–89 good, 90 or more excellent. A faster recovery means lower counts and a higher index.

check.q: A subject steps for 240 s; counts are 70, 60 and 55. What is the PFI and rating?

practice.q: Compared with a sedentary person, a trained person's resting heart rate is:
practice.why: Bigger stroke volume, fewer beats needed.

practice.q: A PFI of 84 is rated:
Put the physical condition ratings in order, lowest PFI first
Write the PFI formula.
practice.a: PFI = duration of exercise (s) × 100 ÷ (2 × sum of the three recovery pulse counts).

practice.q: What step heights and rate does the Harvard step test use?
practice.a: 20 in for people 5 ft 8 in or taller, 16 in for shorter; 30 step cycles per minute for 3–5 min.

practice.q: Why is faster heart rate recovery a sign of fitness?
practice.a: A conditioned heart and circulation restore resting conditions sooner, so the pulse falls faster.

practice.q: Name three warning signs to stop exercising.
practice.a: Chest pain, pain radiating down the left arm (angina), and faintness.

title: The 12-minute run and target heart rate
summary: How far you get in twelve minutes estimates aerobic fitness; 220 minus age sets the training zone.
objectives: Describe the Cooper 12-minute run and interpret the distance
Estimate maximum heart rate and the target heart rate zone
takeaways: Cooper test: distance in 12 min estimates aerobic capacity (VO2max).
Maximum heart rate ≈ 220 − age; target zone 60–80% of it.

steps.title: The Cooper 12-minute run
steps.text:
The Cooper 12-minute run test measures how far a person can run or walk in 12 minutes. Because distance depends on how much oxygen the muscles can use, it estimates aerobic capacity (VO2max). Warm up first and hold an even pace.

For adults under 40, more than about 2700 m is excellent, 2300–2700 good, 1900–2299 average, 1500–1899 below average and under 1500 m poor. Over 40 each band sits roughly 200 m lower.

check.q: What does the Cooper test estimate?
check.a: Aerobic fitness (maximal oxygen uptake, VO2max), from the distance covered in 12 minutes.

steps.title: Ratings by age
steps.text:
Physical condition ratings run from poor through below average, average and good to excellent. Over 40 the cut-offs drop: more than 2500 m is excellent, 2100–2500 good, 1700–2099 average and 1500–1699 below average, with poor below about 1400–1500 m.

The same distance can therefore earn a better rating at 50 than at 25.

check.q: A 45-year-old runs 2200 m in 12 min. Rating?

steps.title: Target heart rate
steps.text:
Maximum heart rate (MHR) is estimated as 220 − age. For aerobic training, bodies such as the American Heart Association (AHA) advise working in a target heart rate zone of about 60–80% of MHR for healthy adults.

Example: at 20, MHR ≈ 200, so the zone is 120–160 beats per minute. At 50 it is 102–136.

check.q: Work out the target zone for a 30-year-old.

practice.q: Estimated maximum heart rate for a 40-year-old is:
The target zone for healthy adults is:
A 25-year-old covers 2800 m in 12 minutes. Rating?
A 30-year-old covers 1400 m in 12 minutes. Rating?
Why should you warm up before the 12-minute run?
practice.a: To raise heart rate, muscle temperature and blood flow gradually, allowing a steady pace and reducing injury.

practice.q: Target zone for a 60-year-old?

title: BMI and waist-to-hip ratio
summary: Two quick numbers for body composition, what they get right and where they mislead.
objectives: Calculate BMI in metric and imperial units and classify it
Measure and interpret the waist/hip ratio
takeaways: WHR = waist ÷ hip; high risk above 0.85 in women and 1.0 in men.
Apple-shaped (central) fat carries more risk than pear-shaped (hip) fat.

steps.title: Body mass index
steps.text:
Body mass index (BMI) = weight in kilograms ÷ height in metres squared. In imperial units: weight in pounds ÷ height in inches squared × 703.

The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) categories: underweight below 18.5; normal weight 18.5–24.9; overweight 25–29.9; obesity 30 or more. Example: 70 kg and 1.75 m gives 70 ÷ 3.06 ≈ 22.9, normal.

check.q: Calculate the BMI of someone weighing 90 kg at 1.80 m, and classify it.

steps.title: What BMI misses
steps.text:
BMI assumes an average build. It ignores what the weight is made of, and it is influenced by sex, muscle mass, bone structure and ethnicity.

So it overestimates fatness in muscular athletes, who are heavy for their height, and underestimates it in older people who have lost muscle but kept or gained fat.

check.q: Why can a rugby player have an 'obese' BMI but little fat?
check.a: BMI counts muscle weight as if it were fat; it does not measure body composition.

steps.title: Waist-to-hip ratio
steps.text:
Waist/hip ratio (WHR) = waist circumference ÷ hip circumference. Measure the waist just above the umbilicus and the hips at their widest part.

Fat stored centrally (an apple-shaped body, central obesity) carries more cardiovascular and metabolic risk than fat on the hips and thighs (pear-shaped). Risk: women ≤0.80 low, 0.81–0.85 moderate, above 0.85 high; men ≤0.95 low, 0.96–1.00 moderate, above 1.0 high.

check.q: A man's waist is 100 cm and hips 98 cm. WHR and risk?

practice.q: A BMI of 31 is classed as:
A BMI of 17.9 is classed as:
Which body shape carries more risk?
practice.why: Abdominal fat is linked to heart disease and diabetes.

practice.q: A woman's WHR is 0.83. Risk?
Give the imperial BMI formula.
List the NHLBI BMI categories.
Where are waist and hip measured?
practice.a: Waist just superior to the umbilicus; hips at the widest part.

practice.q: In whom does BMI underestimate fatness?
practice.a: Older people with low muscle mass.
